report:
**Conclusion**
Contrary to your initial impression, clinical evidence indicates that olive leaf extract (OLE) **can** reduce high blood pressure.

### Summary of Evidence

* **Meta-Analyses and Systematic Reviews:** Pooled data from randomized controlled trials demonstrate that OLE significantly lowers both systolic and diastolic blood pressure. A systematic review noted that 1,000 mg/day of OLE reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure by −11.45 mmHg and −4.65 mmHg, respectively (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ptr.8509). Other meta-analyses confirm statistically significant blood pressure-lowering effects across clinical trials (https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/80445).
* **Comparisons to Standard Medication:** A randomized, active-controlled trial in patients with stage-1 hypertension found that taking 500 mg of OLE twice daily was similarly effective at reducing blood pressure as 12.5–25 mg of Captopril (a standard ACE inhibitor) twice daily (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/).
* **Biological Mechanism:** The primary active compound in OLE is oleuropein. It lowers blood pressure by promoting vascular relaxation, partly through calcium channel blockade (https://www.oleaft.com/medical-evidence/).

While systematic reviews emphasize the need for larger, high-quality trials to confirm long-term safety and standard dosing, current clinical trials and meta-analyses consistently show that olive leaf extract effectively lowers blood pressure in pre-hypertensive and hypertensive individuals.
